e-4287.knowledge_point: Finding Two Scalar Factors in a Linear Combination
e-4287.problem:
Consider the picture below. Given that $\mathbf{m}=\lambda\mathbf{n}+\mu\mathbf{k}$, find $\lambda$ and $\mu$.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13931259/assets/b8abf22d14f93a38c4d01f368b8171e4ccfe90086d932f5b58453baa46391405.png)
e-4287.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13931259/assets/76b9867a7c1ef484922241ebe44272f0104e406c31310bf36227a13850f50d8b.png)

In $\bigtriangleup ONM$ shown above, we have:

- $ON=2|\mathbf{n}|$;

- $\overrightarrow{ON}$ and $\mathbf{n}$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overrightarrow{ON}=2\mathbf{n}$.

Similarly:

- $NM=2|\mathbf{k}|$

- $\overrightarrow{NM}$ and $\mathbf{k}$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overrightarrow{NM}=2\mathbf{k}$.

Additionally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\overset{\to }{ON}+\overset{\to }{NM} \\  & =2n+2k.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $\mathbf{m}=\lambda\mathbf{n}+\mu\mathbf{k}=2\mathbf{n}+2\mathbf{k}$. 

Since $\mathbf{n} \nparallel \mathbf{k},$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{n}$ and $\mathbf{k}$, we get:

- $\lambda=2$ and $\mu=2$

e-4288.knowledge_point: Expressing a Vector That Satisfies a Ratio in Terms of Known Vectors
e-4288.problem:
Consider the following diagram, where $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf{a},$ $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf{b},$ and $X$ divides $AB$ in the ratio $3:1.$ Find $\overrightarrow{OX}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13931259/assets/678ea2936b8a5b1ded74cb8a0875c629e8be0f7002c98492ebf2e8109fc603ef.png)
e-4288.worked_solution:
From the diagram, we see that

$$
\overrightarrow{OX} = \overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AX}.
$$

We're told that $\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a},$ so we just need to work out $\overrightarrow{AX}.$

First, from $\triangle OAB,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\overset{\to }{AO}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-a+b \\  & =b-a.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $AX:XB=3:1,$ we have

$$
\overrightarrow{AX}=\dfrac{3}{4}\overrightarrow{AB}=\dfrac{3}{4}(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OX} & =\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{AX} \\  & =a+\frac{3}{4}(b-a) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}a+\frac{3}{4}b.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
To find $\lambda ,$ we want to match the expression

$$
c=\lambda a-2b.
$$

We are given that one of the components is $-2b.$ So, we first draw the vector $-2b$ from the origin. Then we complete the path to the point $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13931259/assets/40a0137d6227212db9b7ef9f349029838f3f51398790ec5e1c304e12c3743a0f.png)

Let $P$ be the endpoint of the vector $-2b.$ Then

$$
c=\overset{\to }{OP}+\overset{\to }{PC}.
$$

In $△OPC,$ we have:

- $PC=\frac{1}{2}|a|$

- $\overset{\to }{PC}$ and $a$ have opposite directions

Hence, $\overset{\to }{PC}=-\frac{1}{2}a.$

Additionally,

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =\overset{\to }{OP}+\overset{\to }{PC} \\  & =-2b-\frac{1}{2}a.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $c=\lambda a-2b=-\frac{1}{2}a-2b.$

Since $a∦b,$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $a,$ we get:

$$
\lambda =-\frac{1}{2}
$$

Let P be the endpoint of the vector −2b. Then c=OP→+PC→.

Consider the picture above. Given that $c=\lambda a-2b,$ find $\lambda .$
content.worked_solution:
To find $\lambda ,$ we want to match the expression

$$
c=\lambda a-2b.
$$

We are given that one of the components is $-2b.$ So, we first draw the vector $-2b$ from the origin. Then we complete the path to the point $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13931259/assets/e219cc0b1277058339c182a0849592a245645272eabde16cd241df6d9206691f.png)

Let $P$ be the endpoint of the vector $-2b.$ Then

$$
c=\overset{\to }{OP}+\overset{\to }{PC}.
$$

In $△OPC,$ we have:

- $PC=2|a|$

- $\overset{\to }{PC}$ and $a$ have opposite directions

Hence, $\overset{\to }{PC}=-2a.$

Additionally,

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =\overset{\to }{OP}+\overset{\to }{PC} \\  & =-2b-2a.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $c=\lambda a-2b=-2a-2b.$

Since $a∦b,$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $a,$ we get:

$$
\lambda =-2
$$

EXPLANATION

In △OPR shown above, we have

  • OP=2|p|
  • OP→ and p have the same direction

Hence, OP→=2p.

Similarly:

  • PR=4|q|
  • PR→ and q have the same direction

Hence, PR→=4q.

Additionally,

r=OP→+PR→=2p+4q.

Consequently, r=λp+μq=2p+4q.

Since p∦q, the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients, we get:

  • λ=2 and μ=4

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13931259/assets/601e049067de307ef2321ae9b516d1c7306d837ca0758c080074446a8c54389d.png)

In $△OAC$ shown above, we have:

- $OA=2|a|$

- $\overset{\to }{OA}$ and $a$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overset{\to }{OA}=2a.$

Similarly:

- $AC=2|b|$

- $\overset{\to }{AC}$ and $b$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overset{\to }{AC}=2b.$

Additionally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{AC} \\  & =2a+2b.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $c=\lambda a+\mu b=2a+2b.$ 

Since $a∦b,$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients, we get:

- $\lambda =2$ and $\mu =2$

after.worked_solution:
From the diagram, we see that

$$
\overset{\to }{OT}=\overset{\to }{OM}+\overset{\to }{MT}.
$$

We're told that $\overset{\to }{OM}=d,$ so we just need to work out $\overset{\to }{MT}.$

after.worked_solution:
From the diagram, we see that

$$
\overset{\to }{OZ}=\overset{\to }{OX}+\overset{\to }{XZ}.
$$

We're told that $\overset{\to }{OX}=a,$ so we just need to work out $\overset{\to }{XZ}.$

First, from $△OXY,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{XY} & =\overset{\to }{XO}+\overset{\to }{OY} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OX}+\overset{\to }{OY} \\  & =-a+b \\  & =b-a.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $XZ:ZY=5:2,$ we have

$$
\overset{\to }{XZ}=\frac{5}{7}\overset{\to }{XY}=\frac{5}{7}(b-a).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OZ} & =\overset{\to }{OX}+\overset{\to }{XZ} \\  & =a+\frac{5}{7}(b-a) \\  & =\frac{2}{7}a+\frac{5}{7}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the diagram above, where OX→=a, OY→=b and Z divides XY― in the ratio XZ:ZY=5:2. Find OZ→.

a
OZ→=17a−67b
b
OZ→=27a+57b
c
OZ→=27a−57b
d
OZ→=27a+67b
e
OZ→=17a+67b
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

From the diagram, we see that OZ→=OX→+XZ→.

We're told that OX→=a, so we just need to work out XZ→.

First, from △OXY, we have

XY→=XO→+OY→=−OX→+OY→=−a+b=b−a.

Since XZ:ZY=5:2, we have

XZ→=57XY→=57(b−a).

Therefore,

OZ→=OX→+XZ→=a+57(b−a)=27a+57b.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13931259/assets/2f0d9df3316615646dfbd994a378293dacf937050514080b5fe66af9794ae9e3.png)

Consider the diagram above, where $\overset{\to }{OX}=a,$ $\overset{\to }{OY}=b$ and $Z$ divides $\overset{―}{XY}$ in the ratio $XZ:ZY=5:2.$ Find $\overset{\to }{OZ}.$
content.worked_solution:
From the diagram, we see that

$$
\overset{\to }{OZ}=\overset{\to }{OX}+\overset{\to }{XZ}.
$$

We're told that $\overset{\to }{OX}=a,$ so we just need to work out $\overset{\to }{XZ}.$

First, from $△OXY,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{XY} & =\overset{\to }{XO}+\overset{\to }{OY} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OX}+\overset{\to }{OY} \\  & =-a+b \\  & =b-a.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $XZ:ZY=5:2,$ we have

$$
\overset{\to }{XZ}=\frac{5}{7}\overset{\to }{XY}=\frac{5}{7}(b-a).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OZ} & =\overset{\to }{OX}+\overset{\to }{XZ} \\  & =a+\frac{5}{7}(b-a) \\  & =\frac{2}{7}a+\frac{5}{7}b.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13931259/assets/040127594f639248736d4492f1853bcb1e6ef18c37db9242ebe466045713628a.png)

Consider the diagram above, where $\overset{\to }{OU}=u,$ $\overset{\to }{OV}=v$ and $W$ divides $\overset{―}{UV}$ in the ratio $UW:WV=2:7.$ Find $\overset{\to }{OW}.$
after.worked_solution:
From the diagram, we see that

$$
\overset{\to }{OW}=\overset{\to }{OU}+\overset{\to }{UW}.
$$

We're told that $\overset{\to }{OU}=u,$ so we just need to work out $\overset{\to }{UW}.$

First, from $△OUV,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{UV} & =\overset{\to }{UO}+\overset{\to }{OV} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OU}+\overset{\to }{OV} \\  & =-u+v \\  & =v-u.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $UW:WV=2:7,$ we have

$$
\overset{\to }{UW}=\frac{2}{9}\overset{\to }{UV}=\frac{2}{9}(v-u).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OW} & =\overset{\to }{OU}+\overset{\to }{UW} \\  & =u+\frac{2}{9}(v-u) \\  & =\frac{7}{9}u+\frac{2}{9}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the diagram above, where OU→=u, OV→=v and W divides UV― in the ratio UW:WV=2:7. Find OW→.

a
OW→=23u+13v
b
OW→=13u+23v
c
OW→=79u+29v
d
OW→=−13v+23u
e
OW→=79v−29u
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

From the diagram, we see that OW→=OU→+UW→.

We're told that OU→=u, so we just need to work out UW→.

First, from △OUV, we have

UV→=UO→+OV→=−OU→+OV→=−u+v=v−u.

Since UW:WV=2:7, we have

UW→=29UV→=29(v−u).

Therefore,

OW→=OU→+UW→=u+29(v−u)=79u+29v.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms OW=u+(2/9)(v-u)=(7/9)u+(2/9)v, which matches option c.

content.knowledge_point: Expressing a Vector That Satisfies a Ratio in Terms of Known Vectors
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13931259/assets/040127594f639248736d4492f1853bcb1e6ef18c37db9242ebe466045713628a.png)

Consider the diagram above, where $\overset{\to }{OU}=u,$ $\overset{\to }{OV}=v$ and $W$ divides $\overset{―}{UV}$ in the ratio $UW:WV=2:7.$ Find $\overset{\to }{OW}.$
content.worked_solution:
From the diagram, we see that

$$
\overset{\to }{OW}=\overset{\to }{OU}+\overset{\to }{UW}.
$$

We're told that $\overset{\to }{OU}=u,$ so we just need to work out $\overset{\to }{UW}.$

First, from $△OUV,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{UV} & =\overset{\to }{UO}+\overset{\to }{OV} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OU}+\overset{\to }{OV} \\  & =-u+v \\  & =v-u.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $UW:WV=2:7,$ we have

$$
\overset{\to }{UW}=\frac{2}{9}\overset{\to }{UV}=\frac{2}{9}(v-u).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OW} & =\overset{\to }{OU}+\overset{\to }{UW} \\  & =u+\frac{2}{9}(v-u) \\  & =\frac{7}{9}u+\frac{2}{9}v.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13931259/assets/4205d878409776be6c18735910a2f8ece019418452df83cb75d197531f057532.png)

Consider the diagram above, where $\overset{\to }{OA}=a,$ $\overset{\to }{OB}=b$ and $T$ divides $\overset{―}{AB}$ in the ratio $AT:TB=1:6.$ Find $\overset{\to }{OT}.$
after.worked_solution:
From the diagram, we see that

$$
\overset{\to }{OT}=\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{AT}.
$$

We're told that $\overset{\to }{OA}=a,$ so we just need to work out $\overset{\to }{AT}.$

First, from $△OAB,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\overset{\to }{AO}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-a+b \\  & =b-a.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $AT:TB=1:6,$ we have

$$
\overset{\to }{AT}=\frac{1}{7}\overset{\to }{AB}=\frac{1}{7}(b-a).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OT} & =\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{AT} \\  & =a+\frac{1}{7}(b-a) \\  & =\frac{6}{7}a+\frac{1}{7}b.\end{aligned}
$$

OT→=67a−17b

OT→=57a+17b
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

From the diagram, we see that OT→=OA→+AT→.

We're told that OA→=a, so we just need to work out AT→.

First, from △OAB, we have

AB→=AO→+OB→=−OA→+OB→=−a+b=b−a.

Since AT:TB=1:6, we have

AT→=17AB→=17(b−a).

Therefore,

OT→=OA→+AT→=a+17(b−a)=67a+17b.

Consider the diagram above, where $\overset{\to }{OA}=a,$ $\overset{\to }{OB}=b$ and $T$ divides $\overset{―}{AB}$ in the ratio $AT:TB=1:6.$ Find $\overset{\to }{OT}.$
content.worked_solution:
From the diagram, we see that

$$
\overset{\to }{OT}=\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{AT}.
$$

We're told that $\overset{\to }{OA}=a,$ so we just need to work out $\overset{\to }{AT}.$

First, from $△OAB,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\overset{\to }{AO}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-a+b \\  & =b-a.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $AT:TB=1:6,$ we have

$$
\overset{\to }{AT}=\frac{1}{7}\overset{\to }{AB}=\frac{1}{7}(b-a).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OT} & =\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{AT} \\  & =a+\frac{1}{7}(b-a) \\  & =\frac{6}{7}a+\frac{1}{7}b.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13931259/assets/45110269c8a1ca9ad80cabc2f6c44592dca781afde7347d9d0a7e3363a76563a.png)

Consider the diagram above, where $\overset{\to }{OA}=a,$ $\overset{\to }{OB}=b$ and $C$ divides $\overset{―}{AB}$ in the ratio $AC:CB=5:1.$ Find $\overset{\to }{OC}.$
after.worked_solution:
From the diagram, we see that

$$
\overset{\to }{OC}=\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{AC}.
$$

We're told that $\overset{\to }{OA}=a,$ so we just need to work out $\overset{\to }{AC}.$

First, from $△OAB,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\overset{\to }{AO}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-a+b \\  & =b-a.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $AC:CB=5:1,$ we have

$$
\overset{\to }{AC}=\frac{5}{6}\overset{\to }{AB}=\frac{5}{6}(b-a).
$$

Therefore,

EXPLANATION

From the diagram, we see that OC→=OA→+AC→.

We're told that OA→=a, so we just need to work out AC→.

First, from △OAB, we have

AB→=AO→+OB→=−OA→+OB→=−a+b=b−a.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13931259/assets/45110269c8a1ca9ad80cabc2f6c44592dca781afde7347d9d0a7e3363a76563a.png)

Consider the diagram above, where $\overset{\to }{OA}=a,$ $\overset{\to }{OB}=b$ and $C$ divides $\overset{―}{AB}$ in the ratio $AC:CB=5:1.$ Find $\overset{\to }{OC}.$
content.worked_solution:
From the diagram, we see that

$$
\overset{\to }{OC}=\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{AC}.
$$

We're told that $\overset{\to }{OA}=a,$ so we just need to work out $\overset{\to }{AC}.$

First, from $△OAB,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\overset{\to }{AO}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-a+b \\  & =b-a.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $AC:CB=5:1,$ we have

$$
\overset{\to }{AC}=\frac{5}{6}\overset{\to }{AB}=\frac{5}{6}(b-a).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OC} & =\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{AC} \\  & =a+\frac{5}{6}(b-a) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}a+\frac{5}{6}b.\end{aligned}
$$
